preamble: Angelman Syndrome  |  UBE3A / Chromosome 15q11.2-q13 Imprinting Disorder  |  Maternal UBE3A Loss of Function  (OMIM 105830)

questions.domain: Developmental delay first noted between ages 3–6 months?
questions.question: Yes – subtle developmental delay first apparent by age 3–6 months; unique features emerge after age 1 year

questions.domain: No clear regression period (developmental plateau, not regression)?
questions.question: Yes – AS shows global delay from early life, NOT a regression after normal development (distinguishes AS from RTT)

questions.domain: Normal prenatal history and unremarkable newborn exam?
questions.question: Yes – neonatal period typically normal; no obvious dysmorphic features at birth

questions.domain: Feeding difficulties in infancy (poor suck, difficulty latching)?
questions.question: Yes – feeding difficulties common in infancy; poor suck, hypotonia affecting feeding

questions.domain: Hypotonia in infancy?
questions.question: Yes – generalized hypotonia in early infancy; improves somewhat over time

questions.domain: Frequent and apparently unprovoked laughing, smiling, and happy affect?
questions.question: Yes – excessively happy demeanor with frequent, unprovoked laughing is the most characteristic and pathognomonic behavioral feature of AS

questions.domain: Excitability and hyperactivity — easily excited by stimuli?
questions.question: Yes – high excitability, hyperactivity, and short attention span are core behavioral features

questions.domain: Hand-flapping or hand-waving movements during excitable states?
questions.question: Yes – hand flapping commonly accompanies excitable behavior; present in majority

questions.domain: Fascination with or attraction to water?
questions.question: Yes – unusual attraction to water (pools, baths, puddles) is a well-recognized specific behavioral feature

questions.domain: Sociable, friendly temperament despite severe cognitive impairment?
questions.question: Yes – paradoxically sociable and friendly given severity of intellectual disability

questions.domain: Decreased need for sleep (reduced total sleep hours)?
questions.question: Yes – AS patients often require less sleep; frequent night waking, early morning waking

questions.domain: Absent or minimal speech — fewer than 2–3 functional words?
questions.question: Yes – absent or near-absent expressive speech is a hallmark; appropriate use of even 1–2 words is rare

questions.domain: Receptive language skills clearly exceed expressive language skills?
questions.question: Yes – receptive > expressive language gap is characteristic; comprehension better than expression

questions.domain: Non-verbal communication preserved (eye gaze, pointing, gestures)?
questions.question: Yes – non-verbal communication more preserved; eye pointing, gestures, picture boards used

questions.domain: No use of sign language or augmentative communication without intervention?
questions.question: Yes – spontaneous signing absent but can be learned with intervention

questions.domain: Gait ataxia — wide-based, unsteady, jerky gait?
questions.question: Yes – ataxic gait with wide base and jerky movements; uplifted, flexed arm posture while walking

questions.domain: Tremulousness or tremor of limbs (especially upper extremities)?
questions.question: Yes – limb tremulousness is a characteristic motor feature; jerky, puppet-like movements

questions.domain: Delayed walking (most do not walk until after age 3 years)?
questions.question: Yes – ambulation delayed; majority walk by age 3–4 years, some remain non-ambulatory

questions.domain: Tongue thrusting, drooling, or protruding tongue?
questions.question: Yes – tongue thrusting and drooling are common; wide mouth with wide-spaced teeth

questions.domain: Uplifted, flexed arms held away from body during movement?
questions.question: Yes – characteristic 'puppet-like' arm posturing during ambulation

questions.domain: Seizures of any type?
questions.question: Yes – seizures in approximately 80% of AS patients; onset typically 18 months–5 years

questions.domain: Multiple seizure types (myoclonic, atonic, absence, GTC)?
questions.question: Yes – AS associated with multiple seizure types; myoclonic and atonic most common

questions.domain: Seizures triggered by fever or illness?
questions.question: Yes – fever-triggered seizures common, especially in deletion subtype

questions.domain: Seizures difficult to control with standard anti-seizure medications?
questions.question: Yes – seizure management often challenging; polypharmacy frequently required

questions.domain: Abnormal EEG with high-amplitude delta activity (2–3 Hz) with notched or triphasic morphology?
questions.question: Yes – characteristic AS EEG pattern: high-amplitude slow waves, often anteriorly predominant with triphasic morphology

questions.domain: EEG abnormalities present even without clinical seizures?
questions.question: Yes – AS EEG pattern can be detected before any clinical seizures manifest; abnormal background in majority

questions.domain: EEG pattern facilitated by eye closure (delta activity increases with eye closure)?
questions.question: Yes – eye closure-induced or eye closure-facilitated rhythmic delta is characteristic of AS

questions.domain: Normal EEG in early infancy (EEG abnormalities develop over time)?
questions.question: Yes – EEG may be normal in first months; abnormalities emerge with age

questions.domain: Acquired microcephaly (normal head circumference at birth, deceleration after birth)?
questions.question: Yes – postnatal microcephaly in majority; most common before age 3; more frequent in deletion subtype

questions.domain: Oculocutaneous hypopigmentation — lighter skin, hair, and eye color than parents (deletion subtype)?
questions.question: Yes (deletion subtype only) – haploinsufficiency of OCA2 gene adjacent to UBE3A causes relative hypopigmentation

questions.domain: Wide mouth, widely-spaced teeth, prognathism in older patients?
questions.question: Yes – facial features including wide mouth, protruding jaw in older patients

questions.domain: Scoliosis?
questions.question: Yes – scoliosis in subset; requires surveillance especially in non-ambulatory patients

questions.domain: Short stature?
questions.question: Yes – mild short stature common; not severe

questions.domain: Tendency to overheat (heat sensitivity)?
questions.question: Yes – temperature regulation issues; heat sensitivity documented

questions.domain: Chronic constipation?
questions.question: Yes – constipation very common; often requiring ongoing management

questions.domain: Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD)?
questions.question: Yes – GERD documented especially in infancy; feeding difficulties related

questions.domain: Excessive mouthing of objects?
questions.question: Yes – oral hypersensitivity and mouthing of objects noted

questions.domain: Reduced total sleep time — waking 2–3 hours earlier than peers?
questions.question: Yes – reduced sleep requirement; early morning wakening characteristic

questions.domain: Night waking, night laughing, or night activity?
questions.question: Yes – nighttime awakening with apparent good humor; laughing, playing at night

questions.domain: Strabismus (ocular misalignment)?
questions.question: Yes – strabismus present in a significant proportion of patients

questions.domain: Hyperreflexia (brisk deep tendon reflexes)?
questions.question: Yes – hyperreflexia common, especially in older patients

questions.domain: No family history of AS (sporadic, de novo — for deletion and UPD subtypes)?
questions.question: Yes (deletion/UPD) – deletion and UPD cases are essentially always de novo; recurrence risk <1%

questions.domain: Family history of AS or related features in maternal relatives (UBE3A mutation or imprinting defect subtype)?
questions.question: Variable – UBE3A mutations and imprinting center deletions can be maternally inherited; recurrence risk up to 50%

questions.domain: Normal maternal phenotype despite being a UBE3A mutation carrier?
questions.question: Yes – carrier mothers of UBE3A mutations are clinically unaffected (paternal imprinting silences their copy)

sections.heading: MOLECULAR GENETIC TESTING — STEP 1: METHYLATION ANALYSIS

questions.domain: Abnormal parent-specific DNA methylation at 15q11.2-q13 (loss of maternal methylation pattern)?
questions.question: Yes – abnormal methylation (only paternal/unmethylated pattern) detects ~80–85% of AS cases (deletion, UPD, imprinting defect)

questions.domain: Chromosomal microarray (CMA/SNP array): deletion of maternal 15q11.2-q13 (5–7 Mb)?
questions.question: Yes – maternal deletion confirmed in ~68–70% of AS; class 1 deletion (larger) associated with most severe phenotype

questions.domain: Paternal uniparental disomy (UPD) of chromosome 15 confirmed by microsatellite or SNP analysis?
questions.question: Yes (UPD subtype) – both chromosome 15 copies from father; ~5–10% of AS; milder phenotype, lower seizure burden

questions.domain: Imprinting defect confirmed (abnormal methylation with normal chromosome structure)?
questions.question: Yes (imprinting defect subtype) – imprinting center defect ~5–10%; can be inherited; methylation abnormal without deletion

sections.heading: MOLECULAR GENETIC TESTING — STEP 2: UBE3A SEQUENCING

questions.domain: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in UBE3A (maternally derived allele) identified?
questions.question: Yes – UBE3A sequence variant in ~11% of AS; maternally inherited or de novo; methylation pattern normal in this subtype

questions.domain: Confirmed maternal origin of UBE3A pathogenic variant by parental testing?
questions.question: Yes – maternal origin confirmation is essential; paternal UBE3A variants do NOT cause AS due to imprinting

questions.domain: UBE3A deletion/duplication analysis (MLPA) if sequencing negative?
questions.question: Yes – exon-level deletions in UBE3A not detected by sequencing alone; MLPA detects additional cases

questions.domain: No evidence of Rett syndrome — no regression period, no hand stereotypies, MECP2 negative?
questions.question: Yes – RTT excluded: AS has no normal period followed by regression; hand stereotypies absent; happy affect unique to AS

questions.domain: No Phelan-McDermid syndrome features (normal chromosome 22q13 / SHANK3)?
questions.question: Yes – Phelan-McDermid shares absent speech and hypotonia; distinguished by chromosome 22q13 deletion

questions.domain: No Mowat-Wilson syndrome features (normal ZEB2)?
questions.question: Yes – Mowat-Wilson has happy affect, seizures, and constipation overlap; ZEB2 testing distinguishes

questions.domain: No Pitt-Hopkins syndrome features (normal TCF4)?
questions.question: Yes – Pitt-Hopkins has breathing dysregulation and happy affect overlap; TCF4 testing distinguishes

questions.domain: No Christianson syndrome features (normal SLC9A6)?
questions.question: Yes – Christianson syndrome (X-linked) has significant AS overlap including happy affect; distinguished by sequencing

questions.domain: No BEXS/HNRNPH2 variant (excludes RTT mimic with overlapping features)?
questions.question: Yes – BEXS/HNRNPH2-NDD excluded; does not have happy demeanor or characteristic AS EEG

questions.domain: No Prader-Willi syndrome features (normal paternal 15q11-q13)?
questions.question: Yes – PWS also involves 15q11-q13 but affects paternal allele; methylation analysis distinguishes PWS from AS

sections.heading:
Clinical History: No additional cost (obtained during patient encounter and caregiver interview)
Clinical Exam: No additional cost (physical and dysmorphology examination by clinician)
Medium: $300–1,500 (EEG — essential, characteristic pattern; spine X-ray; ophthalmology)
Large: $3,000–12,000+ (DNA methylation analysis at 15q11.2-q13; chromosomal microarray/SNP array for deletion characterization; UBE3A sequencing + MLPA; UPD testing by microsatellite or SNP; parental confirmation studies)

Abnormal methylation at 15q11.2-q13 (25 points) — DEFINITIVE MOLECULAR DIAGNOSIS (80–85% of AS)
Maternal 15q11.2-q13 deletion on CMA/SNP array (15 points) — CONFIRMS DELETION SUBTYPE (~68–70% of AS)
Pathogenic UBE3A variant (maternally derived) (20 points) — DEFINITIVE for UBE3A mutation subtype (~11%)
Frequent and unprovoked laughing/happy affect (14 points) — PATHOGNOMONIC BEHAVIORAL FEATURE
Maternal UBE3A variant confirmed by parental testing (8 points) — ESSENTIAL CONFIRMATION
Paternal UPD chromosome 15 confirmed (8 points) — CONFIRMS UPD SUBTYPE (~5–10%)
Imprinting center defect confirmed (8 points) — CONFIRMS IMPRINTING DEFECT SUBTYPE (~5–10%)
Absent/minimal speech (<2 functional words) (12 points) — ESSENTIAL CLINICAL FEATURE
Seizures in ~80% of patients (10 points) — MAJOR FEATURE
Gait ataxia with puppet-like tremulousness (10 points) — ESSENTIAL CLINICAL FEATURE
Characteristic high-amplitude delta EEG with triphasic pattern (12 points) — HIGHLY SPECIFIC FINDING
No prior regression period (unlike RTT) (8 points) — KEY DIFFERENTIATOR
Acquired microcephaly (8 points) — IMPORTANT SUPPORTING FEATURE
Consensus Clinical Diagnostic Criteria (Williams et al. 2006 / Angelman Syndrome Foundation)

CONSISTENT FEATURES (100% of AS patients — all should be present):
  1. Developmental delay — functionally severe
  2. Speech impairment — absent or minimal; nonverbal communication better than verbal
  3. Movement/balance disorder — gait ataxia, tremulous limb movements, or both
  4. Behavioral uniqueness — happy demeanor; frequent laughing/smiling; easily excited; hand flapping; hyperactive; short attention span

FREQUENT FEATURES (>80% of AS patients):
  • Delayed, disproportionate growth in head circumference → microcephaly (usually by age 2)
  • Seizures — onset before age 3 in most; multiple types
  • Abnormal EEG — characteristic large amplitude slow-spike waves

ASSOCIATED FEATURES (20–80% of AS patients):
  • Flat occiput; occipital groove
  • Protruding tongue, tongue thrusting, drooling, wide mouth
  • Wide-spaced teeth
  • Hypopigmented skin/eyes/hair relative to family members (deletion subtype)
  • Strabismus
  • Hyperreflexia; uplifted, flexed arm posture during ambulation
  • Increased sensitivity to heat
  • Abnormal sleep-wake cycles; decreased need for sleep
  • Fascination with water
  • Abnormal food-related behaviors; obesity in adults
Diagnostic Strategy by Cost — Recommended Testing Sequence

Phase 1 — Clinical Evaluation (No Cost):
  • Apply Williams 2006 criteria: confirm all 4 consistent features (DD, absent speech, movement disorder, happy demeanor)
  • Careful exclusion of regression history (absence of regression distinguishes AS from RTT)
  • Behavioral observation: laughing, excitability, water attraction, hand flapping
  • Family history: maternal relatives for UBE3A carriers; any AS history
  Potential: 50–70 points for $0

Phase 2 — EEG (Essential, $300–800):
  • EEG with eye-open/eye-closure protocol — characteristic high-amplitude delta with triphasic morphology
  • Abnormal EEG pattern present even without clinical seizures; positive EEG adds 12–22 points

Phase 3 — Molecular Genetic Testing ($3,000–12,000+):
  • STEP 1: DNA methylation analysis at 15q11.2-q13 (first-line; detects ~80–85%)
    → If abnormal: chromosomal microarray/SNP array to characterize deletion vs. UPD vs. imprinting defect
    → If deletion confirmed: classify class 1 vs. class 2 (severity correlation)
  • STEP 2: If methylation NORMAL → UBE3A sequence analysis + MLPA deletion analysis (~11% of AS)
  • STEP 3: If UBE3A negative → Rett/Angelman multigene panel or whole exome sequencing
  • Parental testing: maternal UBE3A carrier testing essential when UBE3A mutation or imprinting defect found
  Adding: 40–60 points — crosses diagnostic threshold in nearly all true AS cases

• AS is caused by loss of function of the MATERNALLY derived UBE3A allele ONLY — the paternal UBE3A copy is silenced by genomic imprinting in neurons; this explains why only maternal deletions/mutations cause AS
• Prevalence: 1 in 12,000–20,000; affects males and females equally (unlike RTT)
• Four genetic subtypes with different recurrence risks:
   - Deletion (~68–70%): recurrence <1%; most severe phenotype; seizure burden highest; hypopigmentation present
   - UPD (~5–10%): recurrence <1%; milder phenotype; less severe seizures; normal pigmentation
   - Imprinting defect (~5–10%): recurrence UP TO 50% if imprinting center deletion inherited; milder phenotype
   - UBE3A point mutation (~11%): recurrence UP TO 50% if maternally inherited; carrier mothers unaffected
   - Unknown mechanism (~10%): cannot be confirmed by standard testing
• The HAPPY AFFECT is the most disease-specific clinical feature — not seen in RTT, BEXS, or most other NDDs; its presence should immediately prompt AS evaluation
• EEG is a highly valuable and under-utilized diagnostic tool in AS — the characteristic pattern should prompt methylation testing even before clinical seizures develop
• MANAGEMENT: no disease-modifying treatment approved; active UBE3A reinstatement gene therapy trials ongoing (antisense oligonucleotides, CRISPR unsilencing of paternal UBE3A)
• Genetic counseling complexity: recurrence risk varies from <1% (deletion/UPD) to 50% (UBE3A mutation/imprinting defect) — subtype identification is essential for counseling
• MECP2 testing should be obtained early to exclude RTT in girls with absent speech and apparent regression

Class 1 Deletion (larger, BP1-BP3, ~6 Mb) — Most Severe:
  • Earlier and more severe seizures; highest seizure frequency; most behavioral features
  • Lowest developmental attainment; most hypopigmentation; most consistent microcephaly
  • OCA2 and NIPA1 haploinsufficiency contribute to pigmentation and additional features

Class 2 Deletion (BP2-BP3, ~5 Mb) — Moderately Severe:
  • Slightly milder than Class 1; all consistent features still present

Paternal UPD — Milder Phenotype:
  • Less severe seizures; better prognosis for ambulation; normal pigmentation
  • May have Prader-Willi features transiently in infancy (hypotonia, feeding difficulties)

Imprinting Defect — Milder Phenotype:
  • Least severe seizures; better language acquisition; some develop limited speech
  • Can be inherited — imprinting center (IC) deletion may be maternally transmitted

UBE3A Point Mutation — Variable Phenotype:
  • Variable severity; may be milder than deletion subtype
  • Can be inherited from phenotypically normal carrier mother

Key Differential Diagnoses:
  • Rett Syndrome (MECP2) — regression + hand stereotypies; no happy affect; girls predominantly
  • Phelan-McDermid (22q13/SHANK3) — absent speech + hypotonia; no happy affect; absent seizures early
  • Mowat-Wilson (ZEB2) — happy affect overlap + seizures; distinct dysmorphic features
  • Christianson Syndrome (SLC9A6) — X-linked; happy affect + ataxia + absent speech; truncal ataxia
  • Pitt-Hopkins (TCF4) — breathing pattern overlap; more prominent dysmorphic features
  • Prader-Willi Syndrome (paternal 15q11-q13) — same locus, opposite imprinting; obesity, hyperphagia

confidenceNote:
🔴  85–100 points: High Confidence — Angelman Syndrome highly likely; molecular confirmation strongly recommended to identify subtype; initiate methylation analysis at 15q11.2-q13 and UBE3A sequencing
🟡  40–84 points: Moderate Confidence — AS probable or possible; methylation analysis at 15q11.2-q13 and UBE3A sequencing indicated; clinical genetics referral; Rett/Angelman/epilepsy multigene panel if initial testing negative
🟢  <40 points: Low Confidence — AS less likely; broaden differential to Phelan-McDermid, Mowat-Wilson, Christianson, Pitt-Hopkins, or RTT
